Q: there are two case_when() in code,the conditions are the same. Is the any way to simplify it A:
  1. Wrap a join solution up in a utility function
  2. Generalise for the case where NA is a kpi value to be assigned (so we can't rely on is.na or dplyr::coalesce for the default)
  3. Retain memory efficiency like @Roland's solution but without {data.table} reference semantics, by using copy-on-write
library(dplyr)

dat <- tibble(color=LETTERS[4:10], price=seq(331L,337L))

# NA kpi_1 at color J
lkp <- readr::read_table("
  color kpi_1 kpi_2
  D     11    A
  G     22    B
  J     NA    X
")

dat |> mutate_from_lookup(lkp, default=list(0, "C"))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   color price kpi_1 kpi_2
#>   <chr> <int> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 D       331    11 A    
#> 2 E       332     0 C    
#> 3 F       333     0 C    
#> 4 G       334    22 B    
#> 5 H       335     0 C    
#> 6 I       336     0 C    
#> 7 J       337    NA X

Not run:

# default is optional
dat |> mutate_from_lookup(lkp)

# can pick which `value_cols` (e.g. if many kpis)
dat |> mutate_from_lookup(lkp, value_cols=kpi_2, default=list("C"))

# also can have (or pick from) multiple `match_cols`

Code:

mutate_from_lookup <- function(
  x,
  lookup,
  match_cols = intersect(names(x), names(lookup)),
  value_cols = setdiff(names(lookup), names(x)),
  default    = NULL
){
  j <- fjoin::fjoin_left(
    x,
    lookup,
    on       = match_cols,
    select.x = "",
    select.y = value_cols,
    match.na = TRUE,
    mult.x   = "first",
    indicate = !is.null(default)
  )
  if (!is.null(default)) j[j[1]==1L, value_cols] <- default
  x[, value_cols] <- j[, value_cols]
  x
}

Points:

  • Identify unmatched rows (for the default values) by an indicator rather than by value NA
  • Only carry value_cols (the selected kpis) into the join, and use copy-on-write for the existing columns (x[, value_cols] <- j[, value_cols]). Thus columns like "price" will remain shared between input and output, not copied redundantly as they would be if we just did a left-join with all the columns.

{fjoin} has a .join indicator and column selectors, and uses {data.table} (but works on any data frames). You could recreate the function in {dplyr} at the cost of a couple of extra lines (to pre-select the columns from each side, and manually create the sentinel) and somewhat slower performance on very large data.

Q: In beforeinput, how are ranges determined for deleteWordForward and deleteWordBackward? A:

Neither the Input Events Level 1 or Input Events Level 2 specs define how word boundaries could be accessed by an event handler. I think it's safe to assume there's no way of doing it that's provided by the browser.

Additionally, I've looked discussions surrounding browser specifications. While not directly related to the beforeinput event, these two discussions are related to word boundaries, and how browsers handle them:

  • Different browser behaviors when moving the caret by one word.
  • Specify Selection.modify()?

The consensus seems to be that browsers each implement word boundary handling themselves. Some let the OS handle it, while others handle it themselves.

As far as using a Regex, that won't work, since some languages require heuristics to determine word boundaries (i.e., Chinese and Japanese sometimes require dictionary lookups for their more complex characters).

Q: Why does 'white dot' badge sometimes appear on the taskbar icon? A:

Caused by unread copilot responses, e.g. minimizing vscode while copilot is still 'thinking' and hasn't yet replied - there are situations where the dot can appear to be stuck.

This appears to be an undocumented feature: https://chatgpt.com/share/69bd947d-b650-8000-a695-aa8f7f72b589

Q: Turn off specific autocompletions that override specific snippets? A:

If I wanted to, I'd probably remove Tab as the "accept suggestion" key. This way, Tab only triggers snippets/indentations, suggestions won't hijack it. You can do that in your keyboard shortcut settings, just search for acceptSelectedSuggestion and remove Tab binding.

And I would also keep auto-complete, but make it manual so there is no interference. In VS Code's JSON setting (file -> preference -> settings), add these lines:

"editor.suggestOnTriggerCharacters": false,
"editor.quickSuggestions": false

I wouldn't recommend just searching and toggling them off in the UI; the JSON gives more reliable control:

But if you really need per-pattern control so badly, then you should create a custom snippet with higher priority and disable any specific extensions.
